FEES MUST FALL OCTOBER 2016

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As violence escalates at universities around the country we look at the way forward

Summary:
In week three it seems that the protesting students, government and the universities have reached a deadlock - the demand: no free education or no education at all. We ask what is the reality - is there money, where will come from and how do move forward and stop the destruction.

Further information:
We take an analytical look at the Fees Must Fall Movement speaking to a political commentator, an economist, a higher education research associate, students and the police.

Press Release:


#FeesMustFall
As violent student protests continued on campuses across the country, and spilt onto the streets this week, the remainder of the 2016 academic year hangs in the balance. But as universities take strain, government seemingly refuses to intervene. Can South Africa afford to meet the unwavering student demands for free education and is there a way forward for higher education?


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Fees Must Fall Protests caused havoc across South Africa for the third week running – the demonstrations have escalated with violence, destruction to public property and looting.

BUSISIWE: There are going to be casualties – in every battle that we fighting we are not yet in the war, the war is yet to come… INT2 M5

LINK: The situation has reached a deadlock – the central demand is free education or no
education at all and if the crisis remains unresolved – it may implode. IMPLOdE LINK

JAY: we have a broken political system at the moment INT1 M1

VO: Political commentator and struggle stalwart, Jay Naidoo believes the issues run deeper.

JAY: The crisis we have in education lead by the fees must fall movement is a
reflection, a mirror of the greater crisis in our country // INT1 M1

VO: Higher Education Research Associate Ahmed Essop says the students frustration is not unfounded.

AHMED: I think in a sense the government has created the crises –// the expectation was created that there would free higher education at least for the poor - and there is impatience – nothing has happened. INT1 M6

LINK: The experts who have crunched the numbers and done the sums – say the idea of free higher learning maybe long term goal – but it certainly one our economy can’t deliver right now // NUMBERS LINK

VO: Economist Lullu Krugel says the money simply isn’t there.

LULLU: The unfortunate truth at the where we are in the economy, government finances and the government shortfall it is going to be very difficult to find the funding to provide the free higher education INT1 M1

VO: It’s not what the protesting students want to hear. Sibahle Ndwayana is a Final year student and has not been to class in the last three weeks.

SIBAHLE: Management saying everything is normal – this is not normal – having water canons – problem getting back to academic programme – problem getting back while so much is going on. INT2 M3

BONGANI: Are the students jusitified?
JAY: Absolutely jusitified -//

VO: But the destructive tactics are distracting from the cause.

JAY: but do not allow, the struggle, your legitimate struggle to be hijacked by elements to bring us in a cycle of violence.INT1 M5 // INT1 M6

LINK: They’re nameless and they’re faceless – behind their masks they have been responsible for the burning and the looting and the throwing of stones, no one here will take responsibility for the actions – instead calling them the militant element of the movement. MASKS LINK

VO: This last week, a number of universities came to a halt – with a strong police presence on campuses around the country.

KRUSER: // We cannot allow anyone to carry on with criminal activity INT2 M3

VO: Lieutenant General Gary Kruser is the Acting Deputy National Police Commissioner – we spoke to him at Wits University – the epicentre of the protests.

KRUSER: Put plan in place – life and property protected, and those that want to go class must be able to go to class //
BONGANI QUESTION: heavy handed
KRUSER: – not on one occasion have we taken action without a criminality taken place

VO: Busisiwe Seabe is one the Fees Must Fall Movement’s Leaders - while she has been arrested five times, she denies being responsible for any of the destruction.

BONGANI: SUPPORT IN PRINCIPLE
BUSISIWE: you can’t police black people’s pain – it’s one thing to condemn them – one way to understand – ok as long as no one gets hurt INT2 M3

VO: Dozens of Students have been arrested and charged with crimes ranging from unlawful protesting to malicious damage to property and even attempted murder – for allegedly setting a building alight while security guards were locked inside.

BUSISIWE: // trying that members aren’t violent – open to other influences – other people UJ, rosebank, homeless – because difficult to instil morale, discipline…. INT2 M4
BONGANI: will you name names?
BUSISIWE: although I know who they are would rather go to sun city than give up my comrades. INT3 M7

VO: Sibahle says the time for leadership is now.

SIBAHLE: We are crying for leadership – they just occupy space – wastage within our government. INT4 M2

BONGANI: Will stopping corruption – stop the wastage?
LULLU: //that will help maybe for a year to provide the funding but unfortunately after that we will have to look at finding other resources // it’s a permanent line item we’d be adding to the budget. INT1 M2 // INT1 M1

VO: DR. DIANE PARKER is from the Department of Higher Education and Training – she points out that higher education is not a basic right.

PARKER: The idea of free higher education for all, I don’t think in terms of our constitution, is on the table and I think that’s something that has to be understood. CLIP TWO 05:25
AHMED: we’ve reached a point where the political elite don’t care – the president is missing in action. // And quite frankly I don’t he cares what happens in higher education INT2 M10

VO: Even though basic education is a constitutional right, it is still hugely under resourced and ineffective says Ahmed.

AHMED: There is an enormous problem with the school system and the quality of the school system – // there’s a gap even in our best schools what people come out with and what they are expected to do in universities and higher education. INT1 M11

VO: Basic education shortcomings are reflected in university drop out rates – currently standing around 40% - that means that only 6 out of 10 student complete their degrees.

JAY – INT2 M1: Revolutionised education

VO: Having a degree is privilege yet still not a guarantee of economic success.

LULLU: if you don’t have a degree you have 40 – 50% chance of being unemployed – if you have a degree – that drops to about 6% INT1 M10

VO: The global university graduate unemployment rate is just 2%

Internationally, a mix of university graduate studies and vocational training makes up the employment sector

LULLU: INT 1 M8 Vocational training

VO: With the fourth industrial revolution knocking – adapting skills training will be key to the future and success of our country says Jay.

JAY: our future is about creating entrepreneurs – giving skills to young people that help them build their own livelihoods // They’ve been trained for jobs that don’t exist any longer – this is the core of the debate we should be having, // INT2 M4

SIBAHLE: //can’t just be sitting around and talking – noting happening. INT3 M3

VO: The reality is that nothing will happen overnight, a long term plan needs to be formulated by all the relevant stakeholders.

BONGANI: What are the scenarios, what can we do?
LULLU: If we want free education while at university – you have to pay it back later – either through higher tax for graduates or later retirement – we’re talking of the 10 – 20% of the population – we can’t make everybody pay back for it. INT1 M16
BONGANI: sTUDENTS DON’T WANT TO PAY BACK
LULLU: if you compare us internationally we are much much smaller in tems of economic size – so it is just not feasible // INT1 M14

BONGANI: what if it the money doesn’t come?
BUSISIWE: if it doesn’t come – we are going to continue INT3 M2

VO: Protests have continued through out the week – with campuses burning, students clashing with police and damage to public property.

JAY: WE are standing at the edge of precipice – if we don’t fix it up – we will fall – all of us as a country INT2 M9




PROMO 1
VO: The fees must fall movement is being clouded by a wave of destruction disrupts classes at campuses around the country.

JAY: Do not allow, the struggle, your legitimate struggle to be hijacked by elements to bring us in a cycle of violence.INT1 M5 // INT1 M6

PROMO 2
VO: With the third week of Fees must Fall protests – classes have been disrupted as protesting students clash with police.

SIBAHLE: There is a problem getting back to academic programme.this is not normal – having water canons –INT2 M3


PROMO 3
VO: The fees must fall movement is at a deadlock – with no free education on the table yet – the situation may implode as protests escalate with violence and destruction around the country.
